summary: Follow-up postmortem focused on the 2026-03-08 production incident where Aurora saw elevated tail latency and partial failures during peak traffic. Reviewed root cause (autoscaler interaction + cold KV cache + quantization rollout), immediate mitigations, and longer-term reliability improvements (runbooks, Dedicated pilot, improved telemetry). Agreed next steps: share traces, run Dedicated benchmark, schedule DR exercise, and provide compliance artifacts.
topics: Incident timeline, root cause analysis, short-term mitigations, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, telemetry gaps, runbook and on-call changes, security/compliance asks, next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know you had a rough week — appreciate your time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya (Aurora): Maya here, SRE.
[00:11] Tom (Aurora): Tom, Platform.
[00:13] Priya (Aurora): Priya from Security.
[00:15] Ethan (Aurora): Ethan, CTO.
[00:17] Samira (Redwood): Samira here, I'm the SE who did the bench last month.
[00:20] Luis (Redwood): Luis, CSM, hi.
[00:24] Jordan: Cool. Agenda: quick recap of the 3/8 incident, RCA we drafted, then mitigations and runway to Dedicated pilot, and security asks. We want to leave with clear owners.
[00:35] Maya: Yeah, top line for our side: we saw a spike in 99.9th latency around 11:42 UTC, about 30 minutes, several hundred requests timed out, error rate went from 0.02% to ~1.8% at peak.
[00:48] Tom: Important note — most traffic was to our customer-facing chat endpoint with long context windows, sequence lengths > 2k tokens for some sessions.
[00:55] Samira: Right, that plus the recent quantization patch you rolled caused higher memory pressure on the nodes — we observed higher GC/churn and a backlog in the request queue.
[01:05] Jordan: Ok, we logged steps in the postmortem draft: (1) autoscaler decision created transient underprovisioning during a traffic ramp, (2) recent quantization variant had a regression on large context memory footprint, (3) cold KV cache + repeated context loads exacerbated tail latency.
[01:22] Priya: Can you unpack the autoscaler bit — was it our cluster or Redwood's control plane?
[01:27] Samira: Short answer: edge case in the scaling policy combination. On Dedicated the autoscaler is in the customer's VPC (in Aurora's setup) but the control signals for model pinning and fallbacks flow through Redwood's routing layer. We had two competing policies: aggressive scale-down + slow scale-up thresholds. When traffic ramped quickly, the policy didn't trigger fast enough.
[01:47] Maya: We also saw a few nodes OOMing after the quantization change, that forced the kube scheduler to evict pods which looked like cascading failures.
[01:55] Jordan: Noted. In the RCA we flagged the quantization variant as a regression — we should have caught this in perf-tests for sequence lengths > 1024. Samira, you ran the bench — why did it miss this?
[02:07] Samira: Our internal bench used median sequence distributions; we had a small long-tail test but the sample size wasn't large enough to hit the regression. Also the KV cache wasn't replicated in the test harness so cache-miss behavior differed. My bad there.
[02:21] Tom: There's also a monitoring gap — some of the alerts fired but paging threshold was set to 1% error rate; we had a lot of user-facing degradation before that threshold.
[02:31] Priya: From security side, our compliance team flagged we didn't get a timely audit log for the control-plane events during the incident. We need immutable audit events for scale/fail events.
[02:41] Jordan: Ok so three big buckets: scaling config, quantization regression, telemetry gaps. For immediate mitigations we recommended: roll back the quantization patch for your prod fleet, bump the autoscaler up to a more conservative policy, enable prefix KV cache pre-warming for heavy contexts, and a temporary rate-limit at the edge for very long sequences.
[02:59] Maya: We rolled back the quantization patch last night, that brought error rate down, but tail latencies still spiked occasionally.
[03:06] Samira: Right — rollback avoids the OOMs but the cold-KV-cache still makes some long requests expensive. We can add a short-term pre-warm on deployments during peak windows. Also we can enable intelligent batching changes to reduce per-token overhead.
[03:19] Tom: For Dedicated pilot, how much isolation would we get — i.e., would we avoid the autoscaler control-plane interaction you described?
[03:26] Jordan: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and you run autoscaler within your VPC — however the routing and model catalog still have control-plane hooks for rollouts, fallbacks, and model variants. We can give you an option to disable automatic rollbacks/variant routing for the pilot so you have full control.
[03:41] Ethan: And cost? If we run Dedicated as a trial for a week with higher headroom, what's the ballpark cost?
[03:47] Luis: We'll produce a cost sheet — rough estimate was in the postmortem: a 2x headroom bump for a small Dedicated pool is roughly equivalent to your current monthly hosted burst spend for a week. Jordan will send a more precise spreadsheet.
[04:00] Priya: On the security asks: we need SOC2 artifacts, MFA enforcement logs, and the audit of control-plane events during the outage window. Can you provide those?
[04:09] Jordan: Yes — we'll share SOC2 and ISO docs, and Samira will extract control-plane logs and the audit trail for 03/08.
[04:16] Samira: Quick note — the control-plane logs have partial anonymization for privacy, we'll provide full event IDs for your security team and we can arrange a redacted copy if needed for compliance review.
[04:26] Maya: Ok. Now longer term — we recommended these reliability improvements in the postmortem: add long-tail perf tests to CI, pre-warm KV cache on deploy, conservative autoscaler defaults and a scaling buffer for peak minutes, runbook updates for on-call, and canary rollout gating for quantization/optimization patches.
[04:44] Tom: We'll want a dry-run of the runbook. We had confusion on when to force a roll-back vs. switch to fallback model.
[04:51] Jordan: Agree — action: Luis will schedule a runbook DR and Samira will join to walk through execution. We'll script the fallback to smaller model variant as a single step to reduce decision friction.
[05:02] Priya: Also request for immutable audit logs for control-plane actions. We need a retention policy of 90 days for those events.
[05:09] Samira: We can export audit events to your S3 bucket or to a partner SIEM — whichever you prefer. We'll include retention config in the follow-up.
[05:18] Maya: For the Dedicated pilot benchmark, what scenarios will you run? We want concurrency, sequence length distribution, and ramp tests.
[05:25] Samira: Plan: baseline (median seq), long-tail (99th sequences > 2k), burst ramp (5x traffic over 10 minutes), cold-start with KV cache disabled, and pre-warm enabled. We'll share the script and results.
[05:36] Tom: Can you simulate multi-tenant noise — i.e., variable background load?
[05:40] Samira: Yes, we'll add a noisy-neighbor baseline and also evaluate model variants with quantization profiles.
[05:45] Ethan: One question — is the KV cache the same across Hosted and Dedicated? We heard 'KV cash' in the notes earlier, sorry that was a typo — are there differences in replication?
[05:55] Jordan: Good point — for Hosted the KV cache is multi-tenant and aggressively replicated; for Dedicated we give you the option to colocate KV cache on the same GPU nodes for lower latency, but that increases memory usage. That's where the tradeoff happened with your quantization variant — colocated cache + quantized model = memory pressure.
[06:12] Maya: So we should test colocated KV vs remote cache in the pilot.
[06:15] Samira: Agreed. We'll include both.
[06:18] Tom: Any blockers on performing the Dedicated pilot?
[06:21] Luis: Need a PO & security review signed; Priya, you mentioned some missing attestations earlier — once we have those we can spin up a pilot cluster.
[06:29] Priya: I'll circulate the compliance checklist today, but I need the SOC2/ISO docs from Redwood first to confirm.
[06:35] Jordan: We'll send that today.
[06:37] Maya: Quick nit: the alerting thresholds — we need lower latency SLO alerts, not only error rate. So a 99.9th threshold would have flagged earlier.
[06:46] Jordan: Understood. We'll provide recommended SLO thresholds and sample Grafana alerts.
[06:51] Samira: Also adding a synthetic canary that hits long-context endpoints every minute would help detect regressions earlier.
[06:58] Tom: Great. On the runbook, can we add explicit steps for 'force fallback to small model' and 'increase autoscaler target to X pods'? I want the exact commands.
[07:06] Samira: We'll draft the commands and include kubectl snippets and the control-plane API call examples in the runbook.
[07:13] Ethan: Ok — high level I'm satisfied as long as we get the detailed traces and we do the Dedicated benchmark. I want a post-pilot review with SLA targets.
[07:22] Jordan: We'll include SLA/latency targets in the benchmark report.
[07:26] Luis: Next call? How about 2026-03-18 for status on artifacts and runbook scheduling?
[07:31] Maya: Works for us.
[07:33] Priya: Works.
[07:35] Jordan: Great. Recap of owners then...
[07:38] Jordan: Jordan sends traces & cost spreadsheet by 3/15; Samira runs Dedicated benchmark and shares results by 3/25; Luis schedules runbook DR by 3/16; Maya provides request IDs by 3/13; Priya confirms compliance gaps by 3/18.
[07:56] Tom: Thanks all.
[07:58] Jordan: Thanks everyone.
[08:00] (call ends)
